newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich shows signs of popularity problems at home.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich shows signs of popularity problems at home.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich, known for his low ratings in national opinion polls, may be starting to have some popularity problems among voters at home, analysts say.

With just over a week to go before the Nov. 5 election, the champion of the Republican revolution has seen his lead over Democratic challenger Michael Coles drop as the race in Georgia's 6th Congressioinal District nears an end.

The Gingrich camp until recently had been touting the results of an in-house poll that gave the conservative leader a commanding 30-point lead over Coles, a multimillionaire cookie magnate who eschews the speaker's confrontational style of partisan politics.

But last week, an independent survey put the Gingrich lead at 14 points. And some political experts say the margin of a widely expected Gingrich victory next month could prove less than that, given his poor ratings among local female voters.

"It's a lot closer than it was two years ago. But if Gingrich can sustain the support he has right now, he should win by 10 points or more," said Merle Black, an expert on Southern politics at Emory University in Atlanta.
In 1994, the year Gingrich led the Republicans to their first takeover of Congress in 40 years, he overwhelmed Democratic candidate Ben Jones by an 18-point margin.
But blamed by pundits for two government shutdowns last winter and distrusted by voters for his Republican Medicare reforms, Gingrich is out of favour with more than two-thirds of voters nationally.
Some of that disaffection now seems to be showing up at home in his affluent suburban district, where only 20 percent of voters call themselves Democrats.

Last week's independent poll, conducted for the Atlanta Journal-Constitution and local ABC-affiliate WSB-TV, showed Gingrich's lead over Coles to be smaller than Republican presidential challenger Bob Dole's 19-point margin over President Bill Clinton in the district.
It also pointed to the same underlying gender gap that has plagued Republican candidates generally this year, putting support for Gingrich and Coles even among women.
Gingrich has shown no sign of concern about the race's potential outcome and continues to run on the legislative hallmarks of his 104th Congress.
"The differences are very, very clear," the speaker said while on the campaign trail this weekend.

"If people want us to continue working towards balancing the budget, reforming welfare, stopping drugs and lowering taxes, I hope they'll vote for me," he said. "If those aren't important issues, then I think they have an alternative candidate in Mr. Coles."

But in a half-hour televised debate Friday, Coles sought to portray Gingrich as a career politician tied to special insterest who has worked to preserve corporate subsidies while failing to follow his own call for term limits.
"We've got a career politician that's been in Congress for 18 years and does not do a very good job of representing the values of the district," the Democrat said later.

Coles, a 52-year-old political novice with a fortune estimated at $30 million, has spent more than $1 million of his own money on television advertising this fall. But he is still up against an immense Gingrich war chest of more than $3 million that has been responsible for a barrage of TV, radio and print ads.

A self-proclaimed conservative Democrat, Coles has taken pains to avoid overt links to his national party, refusing even to say which presidential candidate he will vote for on Election Day, in a bid to attract disgruntled Republicans.

"There is a tremendous amount of Republican support for this campaign," Coles told Reuters. "Newt has really disillusioned a lot of people who think his divisive politics has gotten in the way of getting a lot done in Congress."
